**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 23, verses 1–2**

(p-82) Sūrat al-Mu'minūn (The Believers) is Meccan. It has 119 verses according to the Basran (al-Basriyyīn, the scholars of Basra) and 118 according to the Kufan (al-Kufiyyīn, the scholars of Kufa).

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Indeed the believers have succeeded.﴾ They have attained their hopes. The particle *qad* may affirm something expected (*al-mutawaqqaʿ*), just as *lammā* negates it, and when it precedes a verb in the past tense it indicates that the action is firmly established. For this reason it brings the event close to the present. Since the believers were expecting this from God's grace, their good news was introduced with it. Warsh, on the authority of Nāfiʿ, read *qad aflaḥa* by transferring the vowel of the hamza to the *dāl* and dropping the hamza. *Aflaḥū* (with the plural *wāw*) is read in the dialect of *akalūnī al-barāghīth* ("the fleas ate me"), or it is read as a vague pronoun explained by what follows. *Aflaḥ* with a *ḍamma* is read by *ijtizāʾ* (the dispensing of the *wāw* by means of the *ḍamma*, which is a technical term for abbreviating a long vowel to its short counterpart), and *uflliḥa* is read in the passive voice.

﴿Those who in their prayer are humbly submissive.﴾ They are fearful of God, the Glorified and Exalted, humbled before Him, and they fix their gaze on their places of prostration.

It is narrated that "he ﷺ used to pray raising his gaze toward the sky. When this verse was revealed, he cast his gaze toward his place of prostration." It is also narrated that he saw a man playing with his beard, and he said: "If the heart of this one were humble, his limbs would be humble."

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 23, verses 3–5:**

﴿And those who turn away from idle talk﴾: from what does not concern them, whether of speech or of deed. ﴿Who turn away﴾: because of the earnestness they have, which has occupied them from it. This is more eloquent than [the phrase] "those who do not indulge in vain pursuits," in several respects: making the sentence nominal (جملة اسمية, *jumla ismiyya*), building the predicate upon the pronoun, expressing it with the noun, placing the relative clause (صلة, *ṣila*) before it, and putting "turning away" (إعراض, *iʿrāḍ*) in the place of "abstaining" (ترك, *tark*), so as to indicate that they are wholly distant from it, directly and indirectly, in inclination and in attention. Its basic sense is that it be in a side (عرض, *ʿaraḍ*) other than one's own honour (عرض, *ʿirḍ*). Likewise is His saying:

﴿And those who are active in paying zakat﴾: He described them with this after describing them with humility in prayer, to indicate that they have reached the utmost limit in upholding acts of obedience, both bodily and financial, and in avoiding the forbidden and all that manliness (مروءة, *muruwwa*) requires them to avoid. Zakat (the obligatory alms) applies to the meaning, to the substance (عين, *ʿayn*), and to the primary materials, because the agent is the doer of the act, not the place where it occurs; or it applies to the second (the object) by way of an elided possessive construction (مضاف, *muḍāf*).

﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾: they do not expend them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 6–7:

﴿Except from their wives or those their right hands possess,﴾ meaning their wives or their concubines. The word ʿalā (عَلى, "from/over") is connected (ṣilah) to ḥāfiẓūn (حافِظُونَ, "guard"), as in your saying: "Keep hold of (ʿalā) the reins of my horse." Or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: guard them in all circumstances, except in the state of marriage or concubinage. Or it is connected to a verb implied by the phrase "not blameworthy" (ghayru malūmīn). He said "mā" (what) rather than "man" (who) to treat the slaves in the manner of non-rational beings, since ownership is a common attribute of them. The singular "that" (dhālika) comes after the generalisation of His saying: ﴿And those who turn away from idle talk,﴾ because physical intimacy is the most desirable of pleasures to the soul and the greatest in its importance.

﴿For they are not blameworthy,﴾ the pronoun refers to ḥāfiẓūn, or to whatever the exception implies: that is, if they give them to their wives or their female slaves, then they are not blameworthy for that.

﴿But whoever seeks beyond that,﴾ the excepted matter. ﴿Those are the transgressors,﴾ those who are complete in transgression.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 8–9:

﴿And those who are, regarding their trusts and their covenant, [ones who] keep [them]﴾: that is, what they are entrusted with and what they make a covenant about, whether concerning the right of God or the right of creation. ﴿Keep﴾: they are ones who maintain (qa'imun) the safeguarding and upkeep of them. Ibn Kathir read "li-amanatihim" here and in "al-Ma'arij" in the singular, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity (li-amn al-iltibas), or because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar).

﴿And those who, over their prayers, are constant﴾: they are persistent in them and perform them at their appointed times. The verbal form used here indicates the renewal and repetition inherent in prayer, and for this reason everyone other than Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it in the plural (salawatihim). This is not a repetition of what He described them with at the beginning, for humility (khushu') in prayer is other than maintaining (al-muhafazah) it. Opening and closing the descriptions with the matter of prayer is an exalting of its status.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 10–11:

﴿Those﴾ are the ones who combine these attributes. ﴿They are the inheritors﴾, deserving to be called inheritors (wurrath) above all others.

﴿Who will inherit Paradise (al-Firdaws)﴾: this is an explanation of what they inherit, and a restriction of the inheritance after its generality, to magnify it and to emphasize it. The word "inherit" is used figuratively for their deserving Paradise on account of their deeds, although, according to His promise, it is by His grace and in a hyperbolic sense. It is said that they inherit from the disbelievers their dwellings in it, since they forfeited them for themselves, because God Most High created for every person a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in Hell. ﴿They will abide therein forever﴾: the pronoun is feminine because Firdaws is the name of Paradise or of its highest level.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 12–13:

﴿And We certainly created man from an extract (sulala) of clay.﴾ "An extract" (min khulasa) drawn out from among the dregs. ﴿From clay﴾ — "from" (min) is connected to an omitted element, since it is a qualifier of "sulala"; or the min is explanatory (bayaniyya); or it is taken in the sense of "sulala," because the word carries the meaning of "maslula" (that which is drawn out), in which case it is initial (ibtida'iyya) like the first min. The human being here is Adam, peace be upon him, who was created from a choice portion drawn out of the clay; or the reference is to the species, since they were created from extracts that were made into drops of fluid (nutfa) after successive stages.

It is also said that what is meant by "clay" is Adam, because he was created from it, and "sulala" is his seed (nutfa).

﴿Then We made him﴾ — that is, "Then We made his offspring," the word for offspring being omitted (the mudaf is elided). ﴿A drop of fluid (nutfa)﴾ — by creating him from it, or: "Then We made the extract a drop of fluid." The pronoun is masculine in accordance with interpreting it as "the substance," or "that which is drawn out," or "the water." ﴿In a secure lodging﴾ — a firm, well-protected resting place, meaning the womb. It is originally a qualifier of the "resting place," but the place itself was described with it for emphasis, just as it was expressed by the word "qarar" (lodging).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 14–16:

﴿Then We made the drop into a clinging clot,﴾ by turning the white drop into a red clinging clot. ﴿Then We made the clot into a lump,﴾ meaning We made it a piece of flesh. ﴿Then We made the lump into bones,﴾ by hardening it. ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh,﴾ from what remained of the lump, or from what We caused to grow upon it, from what reaches it. The variation in the conjunctions (fa and thumma) reflects the difference between the stages of transformation (istihalat). The plural (al-'izam, "the bones") and the singular (al-'azm, "the bone") are used with respect to their differing form and hardness. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read both words in the singular (al-tawhid), relying on the generic noun (ism al-jins, the noun denoting a kind) in place of the plural. It has also been read with one of them in the singular and the other in the plural. ﴿Then We produced him as another creation.﴾ This is the form of the body, or the soul, or the faculties through His breathing into it, or all of these together. The particle "thumma" (then) indicates the difference between the two creations. Abu Hanifa used this verse as evidence that whoever usurps an egg which then hatches in his possession is liable for the value of the egg and not the chick, since the chick is "another creation." ﴿So blessed is Allah,﴾ exalted is His majesty in His power and wisdom. ﴿the best of creators,﴾ the best of those who determine measures. The specifier (al-mumayyiz, the word that clarifies the comparison) has been omitted, since "the creators" indicates it.

﴿Then after that you are indeed going to die,﴾ certainly heading toward death without doubt. For this reason the descriptive form denoting permanence (al-na't alladhi lil-thubut, i.e., mayyitun) is used rather than the active participle (ism al-fa'il), though it has also been read with the active participle.

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection you will indeed be raised up,﴾ for reckoning and recompense.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 17:

﴿And We have created above you seven paths﴾ — (meaning) heavens, because they are layered (ṭūriqa), some of them above others, like the stacking of one sandal upon another (muṭāraqata al-na'l bi'l-na'l), and everything placed above another is its "ṭarīq" (path/layer). Or, because they are the paths of the angels, or because the stars travel in them (fīhā masīruhā).

﴿And We were not unaware of the creation﴾ — of that created thing which is the heavens, or of all created things.

﴿Unaware﴾ — neglecting their affairs. Rather, We preserve them from ceasing and disorder, and We manage their affairs until they reach the perfection that has been decreed for them, in accordance with what wisdom requires and what the divine will has determined.

Anwar al-Tanzil (Baydawi's Commentary) on Surah 23, verses 18–19:

﴿And We sent down water from the sky in a measure﴾ — in a measure whose benefit is abundant and whose harm is little; or in the quantity of what We knew to be good for them.

﴿And We caused it to settle﴾ — We made it fixed and stable ﴿in the earth﴾. ﴿And indeed We are able to take it away﴾ — to remove it, by causing it to become corrupt, or to evaporate, or to sink deep so that it becomes impossible to extract ﴿We are indeed able﴾ — just as We were able to send it down. The indefiniteness of "dhahab" (taking away, ) indicates the multiplicity of its ways and an emphasis on the threat concerning it; for this reason it was made more eloquent than His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, who would bring you flowing water?﴾

﴿Then We produced for you thereby﴾ — by the water — ﴿gardens of palm trees and grapevines﴾ — for you therein, in the gardens — ﴿in them there is much fruit﴾ — which you enjoy ﴿and from them﴾ — from the gardens, their fruits and their crops — ﴿you eat﴾ — eating for nourishment, or you earn your livelihood and obtain your sustenance, from the saying of them: "So-and-so eats from his trade" (ya'kulu min hirfatihi). It is also permissible that the two pronouns refer to the "palm trees" and the "grapevines," meaning: for you in their produce are kinds of fruit — fresh dates, grapes, dates, raisins, syrup, date-honey, and other things — and food which you eat.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿وَشَجَرَةً﴾ ("and a tree") is conjoined (ʿaṭf, grammatical coordination) to ﴿جَنّاتٍ﴾ ("gardens"). It has also been read in the nominative, as a new sentence (ibtidāʾ, the inchoative), meaning: "and from what We have produced for you by it is a tree." ﴿تَخْرُجُ مِن طُورِ سَيْناءَ﴾ ("that grows out of Mount Sinai"): the mountain of Mūsā (ﷺ), between Egypt and Ayla. It is said to be in Palestine. It may also be called Ṭūr Sīnīn. Either Ṭūr is the name of the mountain and Sīnāʾ is the name of a locality to which it is added, or the two together form a proper name for it, like Imru' al-Qays. Its diptote form (ghayr munṣarif, not taking nunation) is due to definiteness and foreignness, or to femininity by interpreting it as a locality. It is not due to the alif, because the word is of the pattern fiʿāl, like Dīmās, derived from al-sīnāʾ with a long vowel, meaning "elevation," or with a short vowel, meaning "light." Alternatively, it is an extension (mulḥaq) of fiʿlāl, like ʿIlbāʾ, derived from al-sīn, since there is no faʿlāʾ with the feminine alif. This differs from Sīnāʾ according to the reading of the Kufans, al-Shāmī and Yaʿqūb, where it is fayʿāl like Kaysān, or faʿlāʾ like Ṣaḥrāʾ, and not fiʿlāl, since that pattern does not occur in their speech. It has also been read with a kasra and short vowel.

﴿تَنْبُتُ بِالدُّهْنِ﴾ ("that grows with oil"): meaning it grows accompanied by oil and bringing it along. The bāʾ may be a transitive particle making tanbutu transitive, as in your saying, "I took Zayd (dhahabtu bi-Zayd)." Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb in one narration read ﴿تُنْبِتُ﴾ ("produces"). This is either from anbata, with the meaning of nabata, as in the verse of Zuhayr:

"I saw those in need at their tents,
their companions, until the herbage grew (anbata al-baqlu)."

Or it is by implying the subject, "its olive (zaytūnuhā) grows accompanied by oil." It has also been read in the passive voice, which is like the first. It has been read as tuthmiru bi-l-duhn, takhruju bi-l-duhn, tukhriju al-duhn, and tanbutu bi-l-dihān.

﴿وَصِبْغٍ لِلآكِلِينَ﴾ ("and a relish for those who eat"): conjoined to al-duhn and following its i'rab (case inflection). One of the two descriptions of the thing is conjoined to the other. That is, it grows with the thing which combines being an oil from which one anoints and from which lamps are lit, and being a condiment in which bread is dipped for seasoning. It has also been read as wa-ṣabbāghin, like dabbāgh in dabagha (tanning).

Al-Baydawi, *Anwar al-Tanzil*, on Surah 23, verses 23–25:

﴿And We indeed sent Noah to his people, and he said: "O my people, worship Allah"﴾ up to the end of the narrative. It is brought to show the ingratitude of people for the successive blessings He enumerated for them, and what befell them when those blessings were removed.

﴿You have no god other than Him﴾ is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*, a new sentence that is not grammatically tied to what precedes it) giving the reason for the command to worship. Al-Kisa'i read ﴿ghayruhu﴾ ("other than Him") in the genitive (*bil-jarr*), following the wording (*ʿala al-lafz*).

﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾ Will you not fear that He will remove His blessings from you, and so destroy you and punish you, because you abandon His worship for the worship of others and are ungrateful for His blessings, which you cannot count?

﴿The eminent ones (*al-mala'*) among his people who disbelieved said﴾: the nobles, speaking to their common folk. ﴿This is none but a human being like you, who wants to make himself superior over you﴾: who wants to seek superiority over you and to become your master. ﴿Had Allah willed﴾ to send a messenger, ﴿He would have sent down angels﴾, as messengers. ﴿We never heard of this among our forefathers of old﴾: they mean Noah, peace be upon him. That is, we never heard of him as a prophet, or of what he has told us about urging the worship of Allah, exalted is He, and denying any god besides Him, or of his claim to prophethood. This was either because of the extreme intensity of their obstinacy, or because they lived in a long interval (*fatrah*, a gap between prophets).

﴿He is only a man possessed by madness (*jinnah*)﴾: that is, insanity, and it is for this reason that he says such things. ﴿So wait for him﴾: bear with him and wait, ﴿for a while﴾: perhaps he will recover from his madness.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 26–27:

(p-86) ﴿He said﴾ after he had despaired of their faith. ﴿"My Lord, help me"﴾ by destroying them, or by fulfilling what You promised them of punishment. ﴿"Because they denied me"﴾ in place of their denying me, or because of it.

﴿So We revealed to him, "Build the ark under Our eyes"﴾ under Our protection; We shall guard it lest you err in it, or lest some corrupter corrupt it for you. ﴿"And Our revelation"﴾ and Our command and Our instruction of how you should make it. ﴿"So when Our command comes"﴾ to embark, or the descent of the punishment. ﴿"And the oven boils over"﴾.

It is narrated that Noah was told: when water gushes forth from the oven, embark, you and whoever is with you. When the water welled up from it, his wife informed him, and he embarked. Its location is in the mosque of Kufa, on the right of one who enters from the side facing the Gate of Kindah.

It is also said that it was the spring of Wardah in Syria, and there are other views on it that I have mentioned in "Hud". ﴿"Then load into it"﴾ enter into it. It is said: salaka fihi and salakahu (he made him enter), and God the Exalted said: ﴿"What has brought you into Saqar?"﴾.

﴿"Of every pair, two"﴾ of every community, the male and the female, two each, paired. Hafs read ﴿"of every"﴾ with tanwin, meaning: of every kind, a pair, and two, as emphasis. ﴿"And your family"﴾ and the people of your household, or whoever believed with you. ﴿"Except those against whom the word has already gone forth among them"﴾, that is, the word from God the Exalted that he would be destroyed for his disbelief. The particle ʿalā is used here because what precedes is harmful, just as the lām is used where it is beneficial, in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿"Indeed, those for whom the best has preceded from Us"﴾. ﴿"And do not address Me concerning those who did wrong"﴾ by supplicating for their deliverance.

﴿"Indeed, they will be drowned"﴾ without doubt, because of their wrongdoing through associating partners with God and through sins. Whoever is in such a condition is neither interceded for nor does he intercede, and how could he, when He had commanded him to praise Him for deliverance from them through their destruction, by His saying:

﴿So when you and those with you are settled in the ark, say: "Praise be to God, who has delivered us from the wrongdoing people."﴾ Like His saying: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.﴾

﴿Then We produced after them another generation.﴾ They were ʿAd or Thamud.

﴿So We sent among them a Messenger from themselves.﴾ He was Hud or Salih. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 33–34:

﴿The chiefs of his people who disbelieved said﴾. It may be that this is mentioned with the conjunction *wa* (and) because their speech was not connected to the speech of the Messenger (ﷺ), unlike the statement of the people of Noah, where it was introduced as a fresh sentence, thus presuming a question. ﴿And denied the meeting of the Hereafter﴾, that is, the meeting with what is in it of reward and punishment, or their return to a second life through resurrection (*al-ba'th*). ﴿And We had given them luxury﴾, that is, We had blessed them and made them prosperous in the life of this world with abundance of wealth and children. ﴿"This is none but a human being like you"﴾, in attribute and condition. ﴿"He eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink"﴾: this is an affirmation of the likeness. The *ma* here is a declarative *ma* (*ma khabariyya*), and the returning pronoun to the second [*ma*] is either an omitted object in the accusative, or an object in the genitive that is omitted together with its preposition, the preceding clause indicating it.

﴿"And if you obey a human being like yourselves"﴾ in what he commands you. ﴿"Then indeed you would be losers"﴾, in that you would have humiliated yourselves. The word *idhan* (then) is the answer to the condition, and it is the reply to those who spoke among his people.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 35–36:

﴿Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones﴾ stripped of flesh and sinews. ﴿that you will be brought forth﴾ from the graves, or from non-existence, once more into existence. The second "that you" (anna-kum) repeats the first, and is emphasized by it because the separation between it and its predicate has become long. Or "that you will indeed be brought forth" is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the preposed adverbial phrase. Or it is the agent of a verb implied as the response to the condition, and the clause is the predicate of the first: that is, "your bringing forth when you have died," or "that when you have died your bringing forth will take place." It is also permissible for the predicate of the first to be omitted, since the predicate of the second indicates it, and not for the adverbial phrase to be the predicate, because its noun is a corpse (juththah).

﴿Hayhata hayhata﴾ far-fetched is the confirmation, or the soundness. ﴿for what you are promised﴾. Or: far-fetched is what you are promised. The lam is for specification, as in ﴿Hayta laka﴾ ("Come, I am yours" ). It is as if, when they uttered the word of far-fetchedness, it was said: "Why is this far-fetchedness?" They said: ﴿for what you are promised﴾. It has also been said that ﴿hayhata﴾ means "distance," and it is a subject whose predicate is ﴿for what you are promised﴾. It is read with a fatha and nunation for indefiniteness, with a damma and nunation as the plural of hayha, unnunated on the analogy of qabla, with a kasra in both cases, with sukun as the pause form, and with the replacement of the ta' by a ha'.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 37–38:

"She is the soul; whatever you burden it with, it bears."

Its meaning is: there is no life except this life, because "in" (إنْ) is a negative particle that entered upon "hiya" (هي), which carries the sense of "life" and indicates the genus. So it is like "lā" (لا), which negates what follows with a negation of the genus (nafy al-jins).

﴿He is not﴾: i.e., mā huwa (what he is). ﴿but a man who fabricates a lie against God﴾, concerning his claim to have been sent by Him and concerning what he promises us of resurrection.

﴿And we do not believe him﴾: we do not accept him as truthful.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 39–41:

﴿He said: "My Lord, help me, for they have denied me."﴾ Help me against them and take vengeance on them for me. ﴿For they have denied me.﴾ Because of their denial of me.(p-88)

﴿He said: "In a little while they will surely become regretful."﴾ After a short time. The "mā" (ma) is a *ṣila* (a particle that is merely added for emphasis), to reinforce the sense of smallness of the period, or it is an indefinite noun described by a following qualifier (*nakira mawṣūfa*). ﴿They will surely become regretful﴾ for having denied, when they witness the punishment.

﴿So the Blast seized them﴾ The Blast (al-ṣayḥa) of Gabriel (Jibril). He cried out at them with a terrifying cry, by which their hearts were split, and so they died. It has been cited as evidence that the "qarn" (generation) was the people of Ṣāliḥ. ﴿in truth﴾ In the manner that is established and cannot be repelled, or with justice from God, as when you say, "So-and-so judges with truth," or with the true promise.

﴿So We made them into debris (ghuthā’)﴾ He likened them in their destruction to the debris (ghuthā’) of a torrent, which is what the flood carries along, as the Arabs say, "The valley carried him off," said of one who has perished. ﴿So away with the wrongdoing people!﴾ This may be taken as a statement of fact or as a supplication. The *lām* (la) serves to specify the one against whom the curse of distance is invoked. The apparent noun has been placed in the position of their pronoun, to give the reason.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 42–44:

﴿Then We produced after them other generations.﴾ These are the people of Salih, Lut, Shu'ayb and others.

﴿No nation can outstrip its term﴾, meaning the time set for its destruction. The "min" (مِن, "from") is extra (mazīdah), for the sake of comprehensiveness (li-l-istighraq). ﴿Nor can they delay it﴾, meaning the term.

﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession (tatra)﴾, meaning consecutively, one after another. It derives from al-watr (الوَتْر), which is the single unit (al-fard). The yā' (ي) in "tatra" replaces a wāw (و), as in tawlaj and tayqur, and the alif is for the feminine, because "the messengers" is a collective noun. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read it with tanwin, considering it a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the sense of "consecutive," placed as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Hamzah, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i pronounced the alif with imalah (inclination). ﴿Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denounced him as a liar﴾. The attribution of "messenger" (rasūl) is to the sender when speaking of the sending (al-irsal), and to the recipients when speaking of the coming (al-majī'), because the sending, which is the beginning of the matter, is from Him, and the coming, which is its end, is to them.

﴿So We made them follow one another﴾ in destruction. ﴿And We made them into tales﴾, leaving of them only stories to be recounted in evening gatherings. It is a collective noun (ism jam') for ḥadīth, or the plural of uḥdūthah, which is what is spoken of as a pastime. ﴿So away with the people who do not believe﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 47–49:

﴿So they said, "Shall we believe in two mortals like ourselves?"﴾ He used the dual for "mortals" (bashar) because the word is applied to a single individual, as in His saying ﴿a well-formed mortal﴾, just as it is applied to the plural, as in His saying ﴿And if you see any mortal﴾. He did not use the dual for "like" (mithl) because it is in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar). These narratives, as we see, testify that the utmost of the deniers' prophethood-doubts is an analogy between the state of the prophets and their own states, because of the similarity between them in reality. Its corruption becomes apparent to the discerning

(p-89)

upon the slightest reflection. For human souls, although they share the basic faculties and perception, differ in their degrees in these. And just as you see, on the side of deficiency, dullards to whom thought brings no return, so on the side of excess there can be those who are independent of reflection and learning in most matters and in most circumstances, so they perceive what others do not perceive and know what their knowledge does not reach. To this He alluded in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "I am only a mortal like you, to whom it is revealed that your God is one God."﴾

﴿And their people﴾ means the Children of Israel.

﴿who are worshippers of us﴾ meaning servants and submissive ones, like slaves.

﴿So they denied them, and they became among the destroyed﴾ by drowning in the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea).

﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾, meaning the Torah. ﴿That perhaps they﴾ — that perhaps the Children of Israel ﴿would be guided﴾ to the knowledge and the rulings. It is not permissible for the pronoun to refer back to Pharaoh and his people, because the Torah was revealed after their drowning.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 50:

﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign﴾, by her giving birth to him without any touching (*masis*). The "sign" is then one thing referring to both of them. Or: We made the son of Maryam a sign, in that he spoke in the cradle and other miracles appeared from him, and his mother was a sign, in that she gave birth without any touching. The first (the sign attributed to him) was then elided because the second indicates it. ﴿And We sheltered them both upon a height﴾, the land of Bayt al-Maqdis, for it is elevated; or Damascus; or Ramla of Palestine; or Egypt, for its villages are on hills. Ibn ʿAmir and ʿAsim read *rabwa* with a fatha on the *ra'*, and it was also read as *rubawa* with a damma and as *ribwa* with a kasra. ﴿Of firm settlement﴾, a stable place of the earth, level. It was also said: it has fruits and crops, for its inhabitants settle there because of them. ﴿And a flowing spring﴾, and water that is *ma'in*, apparent and running. *Ma'in* is on the pattern *fa'il* from *ma'ana al-ma'u*, when the water flowed; its root meaning is distance in a thing. Or it is from *al-ma'un*, which is benefit, because it is beneficial. Or it is on the pattern *maf'ul* from *'anahu*, when one perceives it with the eye, because by its manifestness it is perceived by the eyes. He described its water with this because it combines the causes of recreation and the goodness of the place.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 51:

﴿O Messengers, eat of the good things﴾ This is an address and a direct speech to all the prophets, not on the basis that they were all addressed with it at once, since they were sent in different periods, but in the sense that each of them was addressed with it in his own time. Thus Jesus (ʿĪsā) is included in it by primary inclusion, and it is the beginning of a speech mentioned as an alert that the provision of the means of enjoyment was not for him alone, and that the permissibility of good things for the prophets is an ancient law, and as an argument against monasticism (rahbāniyyah) in rejecting good things. Or it is a narration of what was said to Jesus and his mother when they took refuge on the elevated ground (al-rabwah), so that they might follow the Messengers in partaking of what they had been provided with. It has also been said that the address is to him alone, and the plural form is for glorification; and "good things" (al-ṭayyibāt) are whatever is enjoyed among the permissible things.

It has also been said: the lawful (al-ḥalāl) is that which is pure in its sustenance (al-ṣāfī al-qawām). So "lawful" is that in which Allah is not disobeyed, "pure" is that in which Allah is not forgotten, and "sustenance" is that which sustains the self and preserves the intellect. ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾ for that is what is intended from you and what is beneficial in the sight of your Lord. ﴿Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do﴾ so I will reward you for it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 52:

﴿And indeed this﴾, i.e., and because (this) and the thing it is given as the reason for: ﴿so fear Me﴾. Or: know that this (is so). It is said that it is coordinated with ﴿what you do﴾. Ibn ʿĀmir read it with the light form (المُخَفَّفَة, al-mukhaffafa), i.e., wa-anna, with the nun unstressed, so it is governed by the preceding clause. The Kufans read it with a kasra, wa-inna, as a fresh sentence (istiʾnaf, resumption of a new sentence). ﴿Your community is one community﴾: your religion (millatukum) is one religion, i.e., unified in belief and the foundations of the laws; or your group (jamaʿatukum) is one group, agreed upon faith and monotheism in worship. ﴿Community﴾ (ummatan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). ﴿And I am your Lord, so fear Me﴾: against splitting the staff (shaqq al-ʿaṣā, causing division) and opposing the one word.

The pronoun refers to what the word "ummah" implies, namely its adherents (arbabuha), the first of them.

﴿And if the Truth had followed their desires﴾ — that is, were there in reality many gods. ﴿The heavens and the earth would have been corrupted, and whoever is in them﴾ — as has already been established in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [21:22].

﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾ — by the Book, which is their reminder, that is, their admonition or their renown; or the reminder they wished for when they said: ﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples﴾ [37:168]. **Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 23, verses 72–73:**

﴿Or do you ask them for a payment?﴾ It is said that this is the counterpart (*qasim*) of His saying, ﴿Or is there madness in him?﴾. ﴿Kharjan﴾ means a wage in return for conveying the message. ﴿But the payment of your Lord﴾ means His provision in this world or His reward in the Hereafter. ﴿Is better﴾ because of its abundance and permanence, so you have sufficient independence from their gifts. The *kharj* (what goes out) is the counterpart of the *dakhl* (what comes in); it is said of everything you send out to another. The *kharaj* is mostly used for a tax on land, and so it implies abundance and constancy, making it more emphatic. For this reason, He used it to express God's giving to him. Ibn 'Amir read ﴿*kharjan* fa-*kharju*﴾, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿*kharajan* fa-*kharaju*﴾, for the sake of *muzawaja* (rhyming symmetry of the two words).

﴿And He is the best of providers﴾ affirms the excellence of His payment, may He be exalted.

﴿And indeed you call them to a straight path﴾: sound intellects bear witness to its straightness, with no crookedness in it that would lead them to accuse him. Know that He, glory be to Him, established the proof against them and removed their excuse in these verses, by enumerating the categories of what could lead to denial and accusation, and showing that none of them applies except the aversion to the truth and the lack of understanding.

﴿And He is the best of providers﴾ affirms the excellence of His payment, may He be exalted.

﴿And indeed you call them to a straight path﴾: sound intellects bear witness to its straightness, with no crookedness in it that would lead them to accuse him. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 74–75:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.﴾ "Deviating from the path" means deviating from the straight path. ﴿Deviators﴾ means those who turn away from it. The fear of the Hereafter is the strongest motive for seeking the truth and following its path.

﴿Even if We had mercy on them and removed the harm that is upon them.﴾ "Harm" means famine. ﴿They would persist﴾ means they would remain firm. Persistence (al-lajaj) means continuing obstinately in a matter.

﴿In their transgression﴾ means their excess in disbelief, their arrogance toward the truth, and their enmity toward the Messenger and the believers. ﴿Wandering blindly﴾ means going astray from guidance. It is related that they were struck by famine until they ate al-'ilhiz (a dish made from blood and hair). Then Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "I beg you by Allah and by the ties of kinship: do you not claim that you were sent as a mercy to the worlds?" He said: "Yes." He said: "You have killed the fathers with the sword and the sons with hunger." Then this was revealed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 78–80:

﴿And it is He who produced for you hearing and sight﴾ so that you might perceive by them the signs that have been set forth. ﴿And hearts﴾ so that you might reflect upon them and derive proofs by them, and (for) other benefits, religious and worldly. ﴿Little are you grateful﴾: you give thanks for them but little, because the essence of giving thanks for them is using them for what they were created for, and submitting to the One who bestowed them without associating anything with Him. The particle ﴿mā﴾ (in ﴿mā tashkurūn﴾) is for emphasis.

﴿And it is He who scattered you over the earth﴾: He created you and dispersed you upon it through procreation. ﴿And to Him you will be gathered﴾: you will be brought together on the Day of Resurrection after your dispersal.

﴿And it is He who gives life and causes death, and His is the alternation of night and day﴾: and their succession is specific to Him, none other can bring it about. This is a rejection of attributing it to the sun in reality, or [it means] that their succession is by His command and decree, or the decrease of one and the increase of the other. ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ by observation and reflection, that all originates from Him, that His power encompasses all possible things, and that the resurrection is among them. It is also read with the ya' (﴿ya‘qilūn﴾, "do they not reason?"), on the basis that the preceding address is to the believers by way of predominance.

﴿Nay, but they say﴾, that is, the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿the like of what the former ones said﴾, their forefathers and those who followed their religion.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 84–85:

﴿Say: "To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it, if you should know?"﴾ "If you should know" means: if you are among the people of knowledge, or among those who know this. This is a way of belittling them and of establishing the extreme extent of their ignorance, to the point that they are ignorant of something as manifest and clear as this. It is an argument that cannot be denied by anyone who has a grain of knowledge. For this reason, He reports their answer before they give it, and so He says:

﴿They will say, "To Allah."﴾ Because clear reason has compelled them, with the least reflection, to acknowledge that He is the Creator of it. ﴿Say﴾ i.e., after what they have said. ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ so that you would know that He who originated the earth and whoever is in it at the beginning is able to bring them into being again, for the beginning of creation is not easier than its repetition. It is also read "tatadhakkarun" (you remember, with the doubled ta'), according to the original form (al-asl).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 86–89:

﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the mighty Throne?"﴾ [It is] greater than that. ﴿They will say, "[It belongs] to Allah."﴾ Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub recited it without the lam (ل) in it and in what follows it, in accordance with what the wording of the question requires. ﴿Say, "Will you not then fear [Him]?"﴾ — His punishment — so do not associate with Him any of His creatures, and do not deny His power over some of the things over which He has power.

﴿Say, "In whose hand is the dominion of everything?"﴾ Dominion (malakut, "sovereignty") is the utmost that can be conceived of as possession; it has also been said that it means His treasuries. ﴿And He protects,﴾ i.e., He gives aid to whomever He wills and safeguards him. ﴿while none can protect against Him,﴾ i.e., no one can be given aid, nor can anyone be prevented from Him; its construction with 'alā (against/over) is because the meaning of support (nusrah) is implied. ﴿if you know.﴾

﴿They will say, "[It belongs] to Allah." Say, "Then how are you deluded?"﴾ — i.e., from where are you being deceived, so that you are turned away from right guidance, despite the matter being clear and the proofs being manifest.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 90–92:

﴿Nay, We have brought them the truth﴾ concerning monotheism (tawhid) and the promise of resurrection (nushur). ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾ in that they denied it.

﴿God has not taken any son﴾ because He is exalted above being like anyone. ﴿Nor was there any god along with Him﴾ who would share with Him in divinity. ﴿Otherwise, each god would have taken away what he had created, and some of them would have prevailed over others﴾: this is the answer to their argument (muhajjah) and the apodosis (jaza') of a conditional clause (shart) that has been omitted, its meaning being indicated by what precedes it. That is, if there were gods with Him, as you claim, each of them would have taken away what he had created and acted independently with it, his dominion would have been distinct from the dominion of the others, and mutual warfare (tahariub) and domination (taghalub) would have appeared among them, as is the state of the kings of this world. Thus the sovereignty (malakut) of all things would not have been in the hand of One alone. The consequence is false by consensus (ijma'), by induction (istiqra'), and by the established proof that all possible beings (mumkinat) depend on one necessary being (wajib wahid). ﴿Glory be to God above what they describe﴾: of offspring and partner, due to the proof already given of its corruption.

﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾: this is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'). Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub and Hafs read it in the genitive (jarr) as an adjective (sifah). It is another proof for the negation of a partner, on the basis that they agree that He is the one alone who possesses this attribute; for this reason He made what follows dependent upon it.

﴿Exalted is He above what they associate﴾ with the particle fa' (fa-ta'ala).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 96–98:

﴿Repel evil with that which is better﴾ (ادفع بالتي هي أحسن السيئة): this is pardoning them and responding to them with kindness, but in such a way that it does not lead to weakness in the religion. It is said that "that which is better" is the word of monotheism (kalimat al-tawhid), and "evil" is polytheism (shirk). It is also said that it is enjoining what is good (al-amr bil-ma'ruf), and "evil" is what is disapproved (al-munkar). This is more eloquent than "repel evil with good," because it contains an explicit statement of preference. ﴿We are most knowing of what they describe﴾ (نحن أعلم بما يصفون): of what they say about you, or of their description of you contrary to your true state, and We are more capable of requiting them. So leave their affair to Us.

﴿And say, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils"﴾ (وقل رب أعوذ بك من همزات الشياطين): their whisperings (وساوسهم). The root of hamz is prodding, and from it comes mihmaz (the goad) of the rider, likening their urging of people to sins to the goading of riders for beasts to walk. The plural (hamzat) refers either to repeated instances, or to the variety of whisperings, or to the multiplicity of what they are attributed to.

﴿And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me﴾ (وأعوذ بك رب أن يحضرون): that they hover around me in any state. The specific mention of the state of prayer, the recitation of the Qur'an, and the arrival of the appointed term is because these are the states most worthy of fear for a person.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 99–100:

﴿Until, when death comes to one of them﴾ is connected to (yasifun, "they describe"), and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) to emphasize the overlooking (of their slander) by seeking refuge in God from Satan, lest he cause him (the believer) to slip from forbearance and incite him to retaliation; or (it is connected) to His saying (innahum la-kadhibun, "indeed they are liars"). ﴿He says﴾ in grief over what he neglected of faith and obedience when he came to see the matter. ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾: return me to the world. The waw (in ur-ji'un, "send me back") is for the honoring of the one addressed.

It is also said that it is for the repetition of his saying "send me back," as it has been said in (the poetic line) "qifa wa-aTraqa" (stop and be silent, where the dual form is used for repetition).

﴿That perhaps I may do righteousness in that which I have left behind﴾: in the faith which I left behind, i.e., that perhaps I may attain faith and act upon it. It is also said (that what is meant is) wealth, or the world.

And from him, upon him be prayer and peace, it is narrated that he said: "When the believer sees the angels, they say, 'Shall we return you to the world?' He says, 'To the abode of worries and sorrows? Rather, a hastening to God, the Exalted.' As for the disbeliever, he says, 'My Lord, send me back!'"

﴿No!﴾: a rebuke against seeking the return and a declaration of its remoteness. ﴿Indeed it is a word﴾: the meaning of His saying "My Lord, send me back" etc. A "word" (kalimah) is a portion of speech whose parts are arranged together. ﴿He is its speaker﴾: without doubt, since grief has taken hold of him. ﴿And behind them﴾: before them; the pronoun refers to the group.

﴿There is a barrier﴾: a barrier between them and return. ﴿Until the day they are raised﴾: the Day of Resurrection. This is a complete despair of returning to the world, since he knows that there is no return to the world on the Day of Resurrection; rather, return on that day is to a life that will be in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 101–103:

﴿When the Trumpet is blown﴾ for the Hour (qiyam al-sa'ah). The reading is with a fatha on the waw, and this (reading) together with a kasra on the sad supports that al-sur (the trumpet) is also the plural of al-surah (the form).

﴿Then there will be no kinship between them﴾ benefiting them, due to the cessation of mutual compassion and mercy, because of the extreme bewilderment and the overwhelming of dread, such that a man flees from his brother, his mother, his father, his companion and his sons, or they boast of them. ﴿On that Day﴾ as they do today. ﴿Nor will they ask one another﴾ about (their condition), nor will one ask another, due to his being preoccupied with himself. This does not contradict His saying ﴿And some of them will turn to others, questioning one another﴾, because that (questioning) is at the (time of the) second blast, and that is after the reckoning, or after the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire.

﴿As for him whose scales are heavy﴾ the things weighed (mawzunat) are his beliefs and deeds, meaning: whoever has beliefs and righteous deeds will have weight and worth with Allah the Exalted. ﴿Those are the successful﴾, the ones who win salvation and high ranks.

﴿And as for him whose scales are light﴾ whoever does not have that which would have weight, and they are the disbelievers, due to His saying the Exalted: ﴿We shall assign them no weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿Those are the ones who have lost their souls﴾, they defrauded them, since they wasted the time of their perfecting and nullified their readiness to attain their perfection. ﴿Abiding in Hell﴾ is either a substitute for the relative clause (silah) or a second predicate for ﴿those﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 104–106:

﴿The Fire scorches their faces﴾: it burns them. Al-laf'h (scorching) is like al-nafh (blowing/touching with heat), except that it has a stronger effect. ﴿And they therein are grimacing﴾: from the intensity of the burning. Al-kulooh (grimacing) is the drawing back of the two lips from the teeth. It is also read as ﴿kalihoon﴾.

﴿Were not My verses recited to you?﴾: this is with the verb "say" implied, meaning: it will be said to them, "Were not..." ﴿But you used to deny them﴾: a rebuke and reminder to them of the reason for which they deserved this punishment.

﴿They will say: "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us﴾: it took possession of us, such that our states led to an evil end. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿shaqawatuna﴾ with a fatha, like sa'adah (happiness), and it is also read with a kasra, like kitabah (writing). ﴿And we were a people astray﴾: from the truth.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 107–108:

﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it﴾: from the Fire. ﴿Then if we return﴾: to denial. ﴿Then indeed we are wrongdoers﴾: against ourselves.

﴿He said, "Be silenced therein"﴾: be silent with the silence of humiliation in the Fire, for it is not a place of asking. [This is] like when I say, "khasa'tu al-kalb" (I drove the dog away) when I shoo it and it slinks off (fa-khasa'). ﴿And do not speak to Me﴾: concerning the lifting of the punishment; or, "do not speak to Me" at all. Then they say for a thousand [years], "Our Lord, You have made us die twice," and they are answered, "That is because when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved." Then they say for a thousand [years], "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us," and they are answered, "Indeed you will remain [here]." Then they say for a thousand [years], "Our Lord, delay us to a near term," and they are answered, "Had you not sworn before that you would never decline?" Then they say for a thousand [years], "Our Lord, bring us out, we will do righteous deeds," and they are answered, "Did We not give you a long enough life?" Then they say for a thousand [years], "My Lord, send us back," and they are answered, "Be silenced therein." Then there will be for them therein nothing but groaning (zafir), sighing (shahiq), and howling (u'a').

It is also said that they were the Companions, and it is also said that they were the *Ahl al-Suffa* (the People of the Bench, poor Companions who lived in the mosque of the Prophet ﷺ). ﴿who would say: "Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy on us, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾

﴿So you took them as objects of ridicule﴾: *huzuwan* (mockery). Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *sikhriyyan* here and in Surah Sad with a *damma* (*sukhriyyan*). Both are verbal nouns from *sakhira* (to mock), with the *ya' al-nisba* (the suffix of relation, which gives the sense of intensification) added to them for emphasis. According to the Kufan grammarians, the form with *kasra* (*sikhriyyan*) means mockery, while the form with *damma* (*sukhriyyan*) is from *sukhrah* and means subjugation and servitude.

﴿to the extent that they made you forget My remembrance﴾: due to your excessive preoccupation with mocking them, so you did not fear Me regarding My friends. ﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾: mocking them.

﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for what they endured﴾: for their patience under your harm. ﴿that they are the triumphant﴾: their triumph is in attaining all their desires, being singled out for it. This is the second object of ﴿I have rewarded them﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a *kasra* (*innI*), as a new, independent statement (*isti'nafan*). (p-97)

﴿He said﴾: i.e., Allah, or the angel commanded to question them. Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it as the imperative ﴿قُلْ﴾ ("Say"), addressed to the angel, or to one of the leaders of the people of the Fire. ﴿How many years did you remain on earth﴾, whether alive or dead in the graves? ﴿A number of years﴾ is a *tamyiz* (a noun of specification, explaining the vague number ﴿كَمْ﴾ "how many").

﴿They said: We remained a day or part of a day﴾. This belittling of the length of their stay is relative to their eternal abiding in the Fire, or because those were days of pleasure, and days of pleasure are short, or because that time has passed, and what has passed is as if it did not exist. ﴿So ask those who count﴾: those who are able to count its days, if you wish to verify it, for we are preoccupied with the punishment we are in and are too busy to recall and reckon it; or it means the angels who count the lifespans of people and enumerate their deeds. It has been read as ﴿الْعَادِينَ﴾ (*al-'adin*) with a light pronunciation, meaning the wrongdoers, for they say what we say; and as ﴿الْعَادِّينَ﴾ (*al-'addin*, with the doubled letter), the reckoners. ﴿الْعَادِّيِّينَ﴾ (*al-'addiyyin*) means the ancient, long-lived ones, for they too consider the time short.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 115:

﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ This is a rebuke for their heedlessness. "ʿAbathan" (in vain, without purpose) is either a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) meaning "playing" (ʿābithīn), or an accusative of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), i.e. We did not create you for amusement; rather We created you so that We might have you worship Us and recompense you for your deeds, and this serves as an indication of the Resurrection. ﴿And that to Us you will not be returned?﴾ This is coordinated with "that We created you" or with "ʿabathan". Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Yaʿqūb read it with a fatḥah on the tāʾ and a kasrah on the jīm (turjaʿūn becoming tarjiʿūn, i.e. "you will not be made to return" in the active sense, read as tarjiʿūna with the verb's vowels altered).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 116–117:

﴿So exalted is Allah, the King, the Truth﴾. He to whom sovereignty truly belongs absolutely; for everything other than Him is owned in its essence (dhatan) as a possession, and owns only by accident (arada) in one respect and not another, and in one state and not another.

﴿There is no god but He﴾, for everything other than Him is His servant.

﴿Lord of the Noble Throne﴾, which encompasses the celestial bodies and from which the firmly decreed judgments and rulings descend. Therefore He described it as noble, or because it is attributed to the Most Noble of the noble.

It is also read in the nominative case (bi'l-raf'), on the basis that it is an attribute of the Lord.

﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah﴾, worshipping him either exclusively or as a partner. ﴿For which he has no proof﴾ is another attribute of ﴿a god﴾, necessarily belonging to it, since falsehood has no proof. It was brought in for emphasis and to build the ruling upon it, as a warning that adopting a religion for which there is no evidence is forbidden, let alone one which the evidence has shown to be contrary. Or it is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraDh) between the condition and the consequence, for: ﴿Then his reckoning is only with his Lord﴾, meaning He will recompense him with exactly what he deserves. ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed﴾; indeed the matter is so (inna al-sha'n). It is also read with a fatha (annahu), on the basis of causation (ta'lil) or as a predicate (khabar), i.e. his reckoning is the non-attainment of success. He opened the surah by affirming the success of the believers and concluded it by negating success from the disbelievers. Then He commanded His Messenger to seek forgiveness from Him and to seek His mercy, so He said:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 118:

﴿And say: "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾

From the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Mu'minun, the angels will give him glad tidings of al-rawh (the spirit) and al-rayhan (the sweet basil), and of that which will delight his eye at the time the Angel of Death comes."

And from him (peace be upon him), who said: "Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever acts upon them will enter Paradise." Then he recited ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ until he finished the ten.

And it is narrated: "Its first and its last are among the treasures of Paradise. Whoever acts upon three verses from its beginning and takes admonition from four from its end has indeed been saved and succeeded."
